newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's McKinnon not prejudging on NZ$94 mln "palace".
newsitem.headline: NZ's McKinnon not prejudging on NZ$94 mln "palace".

text.p: Foreign Affairs Minister Don McKinnon said on Thursday he was happy to see a debate in parliament on a planned $94 million ministerial building.

"We are not prejudging this committee. I am very happy to have it debated in the House, but I am only one of 120 members," McKinnon, the minister responsible for the building, told the government administration select committee.
But he said he did not think moving or demolishing the current ministerial building, the Beehive -- suggested yesterday by property investor Sir Robert Jones -- was a real option.
The committee on Thursday completed its two day hearing in response to a 200,000 signature petition opposing the building presented last month.
It is due to report to parliament before the end of June.
Cabinet in April approved the building, dubbed "the parliamentary palace" by its critics, in the face of strong public opposition to the expenditure and to the demolition of Broadcasting House.
McKinnon told the committee he hoped and expected the final price to be below $94 million.
Apart from McKinnon, only one oral submission -- from a representative of building union workers concerned about jobs -- was in favour of the building.
Manufacturers' and farmers' representatives said the country could not afford to spend the money.

"The New Zealand economy, and particularly the farming and export sector, is struggling, and in a nutshell we can't afford this building," Federated Farmers chief executive Malcolm Bailey told the committee.
"We believe the spending is creating pressures...which are impacting negatively on the economy," he said.
"We have made a lot of progress (with economic reforms) but you are threatening it right now."
Bailey said the downward trend in government spending as a percentage of GDP was welcome but there was concern decisions such as the new building would see that trend stop or be reversed.
Manufacturers' Federation chief executive Simon Arnold said the central issue was the quality of government spending.
"This building has become a bit of a touchstone of the adequacy of government expenditure. It is indicative of the sort of problems we have," Arnold said.
